name: mirage
text: Short answer: no special maker credit for parlays, and it's profitable only in a thin, capital-hungry way. How it works: a parlay buyer pays us a price P and we owe $1 if all legs hit. Our only profit is price minus the true chance, no fee and no rebate (the buyer pays Novig's fee). So we earn the spread: today the market pays roughly 0.6 to 1.1 points of the pot over our fair, per trade, and each parlay locks collateral ($30-100) for days. Parlays are 'profitable' for makers because buyers on average overpay: bettors pay a margin on long shots. But that margin is competed down by professional LPs, ours has to be priced against the same fair, and 1 pt on a $10 stake is $0.10 to $1 per parlay. At $5,000+ of collateral it's real money; at $80 it's a few dollars a week, with variance (we lost 3 early ones for -$7). So it works as a volume business: needs capital and many priceable parlays. That's why I'm keeping it on paper to measure exactly what a live version would earn per $100 of collateral.
